label: thm:prevalence
title: Main Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:prevalence}
For every metric $h \in C^\infty(S^2T^*M)$ of negative sectional curvature, there exist an open $C^3$-neighborhood $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}$ of $h$ and a constant $B=B(h)>0$ such that, for every integer $k\geqslant3$, the set of metrics $g\in\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}\cap C^k(S^2T^*M)$ for which there is $a = a(g)>0$ satisfying the \emph{sublinear sparsity condition}
\[
 |\ell_g(\gamma)-\ell_g(\eta)|
 \geqslant a \cdot e^{-B\sqrt{k}\max\{\ell_g(\gamma),\ell_g(\eta)\}},
 \qquad \forall \gamma\ne\eta
\]
is Borel, prevalent, and hence dense in $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}\cap C^k(S^2T^*M)$.
head: environment
name: Prevalence of exponential gaps

label: geo:sections
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{geo:sections}
There are finitely many pairwise disjoint compact smooth transverse disks $D_i\subset S_hM$, compact cores $K_i\Subset D_i$, and constants $R,\tau>0$ with the following properties. Every orbit meets some $K_i$ in forward time at most $R$, and consecutive intersections with $\bigcup_iD_i$ are separated by at least $\tau$. Each $D_i$ has a slightly larger smooth transverse extension and a fixed flow box. These properties hold uniformly for $g\in\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}$. \qed
head: environment
name: A fixed family of transverse sections

label: geo:cluster
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Extreme neighbours lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first choose the boundaries of the sections away from the orbit hits. Inside each $D_i$, fix a smooth collar with level domains $E_i(a)=\{\rho_i\leqslant a\}$, $1\leqslant a\leqslant2$, containing $K_i$ and staying a fixed distance from $\partial D_i$. By Lemma~\ref{geo:sections}, $\Gamma$ has at most $C(1+T)$ intersections with the full disks. We call these the virtual hits. Removing an interval of radius $c/(1+T)$ about each value $\rho_i(w)$ at a virtual hit leaves a choice of $a_i\in[1,2]$, provided $c$ is small. We take $E_i=E_i(a_i)$. Every virtual hit is then at distance at least $c/(1+T)$ from $\partial E_i$.

The first return $F$ to $\bigcup_iE_i$ permutes $S$, and $N:=\#S\leqslant C(1+T)$. Its branch and return time at each hit are defined in a disk of radius $c/(1+T)$, with Lipschitz constants at most a fixed $A\geqslant2$. Indeed, the next hit occurs within a uniformly bounded time. The nearby trajectory has the same intersections with the sections: their inclusion is fixed by the boundary margin, and their order is fixed by the lower return-time bound $\tau$. The implicit function theorem in the fixed flow boxes gives the asserted Lipschitz estimates.

We now assign a finite alphabet to the hits. A letter records the section, a cell of a fine fixed coordinate grid, and a bin for the next return time. The spatial mesh and the width of the time bins are fixed, independently of $T$. Translating these grids puts their boundaries at distance at least $c/(1+T)$ from the finitely many recorded values. Thus the letter is constant in a disk of this radius about every hit.

These itineraries distinguish the points of $S$ when the meshes are sufficiently small. To see this, suppose two hits $z,w$ have the same future itinerary. Their periodicity gives the same bilateral itinerary. Matching consecutive return times by a piecewise affine time change makes the two trajectories uniformly close: the spatial and time errors on each return segment are bounded by a constant times the mesh size. We decrease $\tau$, if necessary, so that $a=\tau/2$ is an allowed choice in the expansivity statement above, and choose the meshes to make these errors smaller than its corresponding $e$. Expansivity gives $w=\varphi_s(z)$ with $|s|<\tau/2$. If $s\ne0$, this would give two distinct intersections of one orbit with the transverse disks in a time interval shorter than $\tau$, contrary to Lemma~\ref{geo:sections}. Hence $s=0$ and $w=z$.

Let $p(j)$ be the number of observed words of length $j$, with $p(0)=1$. We obtain
\begin{equation}
 p(j)\geqslant\min\{N,j+1\}.
 \label{geo:complexity}
\end{equation}
Indeed, if $p(j+1)=p(j)$, each observed $j$-word has a unique right extension. Since $F$ permutes $S$, successive extensions determine the entire future itinerary, and hence a single hit. Thus equality is possible only when $p(j)=N$; until then, $p(j)$ increases by at least one at every step.

If $N>m$, let $j=\lfloor N/(m+1)\rfloor$. By~\eqref{geo:complexity}, $p(j)>N/(m+1)$, so some word occurs at most $m$ times. Let $\mathcal C$ be its set of occurrences and choose $z\in\mathcal C$. A hit within $c(1+T)^{-1}A^{-j}$ of $z$ has the same first $j$ letters, because its distance from the corresponding iterates of $z$ stays below the boundary margin. It therefore belongs to $\mathcal C$. Since $j\leqslant C(1+T)/m$, this proves~\eqref{geo:sparseball}, after decreasing $c$. When $N\leqslant m$, we take $\mathcal C=S$ and use the boundary margin to choose the ball.

Let us also justify the separation of distinct hits. Put $\rho=c/(1+T)$, with $c$ small enough that every return branch is $A$-Lipschitz and every letter is constant in the radius-$\rho$ disk about a hit. Suppose two hits $z,w$ in the same section satisfy $\operatorname{dist}(z,w)<\rho A^{-N}$. Inductively, they follow the same return branches and
\[
 \operatorname{dist}\bigl(F^j(z),F^j(w)\bigr)\leqslant A^j\operatorname{dist}(z,w)<\rho,\qquad 0\leqslant j<N.
\]
Their first $N$ letters therefore agree. This contradicts $p(N-1)=N$, which says that words of length $N-1$ already distinguish all $N$ hits. Thus
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(z,w)\geqslant\rho A^{-N}\geqslant c(1+T)^{-1}e^{-CT},
\]
since $N\leqslant C(1+T)$ and $A$ is fixed. Distinct compact disks $D_i$ have a fixed positive mutual distance, so hits in different disks satisfy the same bound after decreasing $c$. This proves~\eqref{geo:hitsep}.

Finally, consider two distinct oriented periodic orbits and use the adaptive sections for their union. Flow a point on the first orbit to a core in time at most $R$. A sufficiently close point on the second orbit gives, by bounded-time tracking and transverse projection, a distinct hit at distance at most a fixed multiple of the original distance. The boundary margin keeps this hit in the same adaptive section. Estimate~\eqref{geo:hitsep} therefore gives the claimed phase-space separation.
head: environment

label: geo:graphs
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Short geodesic graphs

label: geo:gronwall
title: Proof
body_md:
In coordinates $(t,y)$, a geodesic graph satisfies
\[
 (u^\alpha)''=-\Gamma^\alpha_{ij}(t,u)w^iw^j+(u^\alpha)'\Gamma^1_{ij}(t,u)w^iw^j,\qquad w=(1,u').
\]
Subtracting the two equations and using the mean value formula gives~\eqref{geo:graphode}. Let us write out the resulting comparison. For $s\leqslant t$ in $I$, integration gives
\[
 |b(t)|+|b'(t)|\leqslant |b(s)|+|b'(s)|+C\int_s^t\bigl(|b(v)|+|b'(v)|\bigr)\,dv.
\]
Gronwall's inequality bounds the right side by $e^{C(t-s)}(|b(s)|+|b'(s)|)$. Applying the same argument backwards in time, we obtain
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 e^{-C|t-s|}\bigl(|b(s)|+|b'(s)|\bigr)
 &\leqslant |b(t)|+|b'(t)|\\
 &\leqslant e^{C|t-s|}\bigl(|b(s)|+|b'(s)|\bigr),\qquad s,t\in I.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{geo:gronwall}
\end{equation}
Since $I$ has fixed length, the comparison factor is uniform.

If the set in~\eqref{geo:sublevel} is nonempty, let $t_0$ belong to it. Then $|b(t_0)|<a<cq$ and $|b'(t_0)|\geqslant q-a$. In particular, for $c\leqslant1/2$, we have $|b(t_0)|+|b'(t_0)|\leqslant2|b'(t_0)|$. Integrating~\eqref{geo:graphode} and using~\eqref{geo:gronwall}, we get
\[
 \sup_{t\in I}|b'(t)-b'(t_0)|
 \leqslant 2C|I|e^{C|I|}|b'(t_0)|
 \leqslant\tfrac12|b'(t_0)|,
\]
where the last inequality follows by fixing $|I|$ sufficiently small.
Consequently the projection of $b(t)$ in the direction $b'(t_0)$ is strictly increasing, with derivative at least $|b'(t_0)|/2$. The preimage of $[-a,a]$ has length at most $4a/|b'(t_0)|\leqslant Ca/q$, as required.
head: environment

label: geo:detector
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: A separating metric variation

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that the geometric geodesics are distinct. Lemma~\ref{geo:cluster}, applied to both orientations of both geodesics, gives a hit $z$ with at most $m$ extreme neighbours at scale $\delta$. After interchanging $\gamma,\eta$ and reversing parameters if necessary, we may assume that $z$ belongs to $\gamma$.

In a fixed smooth chart, followed by a bounded linear coordinate change, write a short arc of $\gamma$ as $x(t)=(t,u_0(t))$, $t\in I$, with $x(0)=\pi(z)$. Here $\pi:S_hM\to M$ is the bundle projection, and $I$ has a fixed small length. Initial data $(u(0),u'(0))$ of nearby geodesic graphs are uniformly bi-Lipschitz equivalent to their hits in the transverse disk containing $z$. Consequently, at most $m-1$ distinct graphs of $\eta$ have initial data within $c\delta$ of those of $u_0$: each gives an extreme neighbour other than $z$. Denote them by $u_1,\ldots,u_q$, where $q\leqslant m-1$. We count coincident passages only once. Including both orientations accounts for passages whose original direction is opposite to that of $\gamma$.

Let us find a point of the main arc away from all other passages of $\eta$. Divide $\eta$ into at most $C(1+T)$ short arcs, with overlapping extensions. An arc approaching $x(I)$ with a small angle in either orientation extends as a graph over $I$. If it is not one of the selected graphs, its initial-data distance is at least $c\delta$. By~\eqref{geo:gronwall},
\[
 |u(t)-u_0(t)|+|u'(t)-u_0'(t)|\geqslant c\delta,\qquad t\in I.
\]
Lemma~\ref{geo:graphs} then bounds the portion of $I$ at base distance less than $4r$ from this arc by $Cr/\delta$. An arc making a fixed positive angle has the stronger bound $Cr$. To see this, parametrize it by $g$-arclength as $(t(s),y(s))$ and put $w(s)=y(s)-u_0(t(s))$. At a point close to the main arc, the angle assumption gives $|w'(s_0)|\geqslant c$. With $e=w'(s_0)/|w'(s_0)|$, the uniform bounds on second derivatives imply $\langle w'(s),e\rangle\geqslant c/2$ on the sufficiently short arc. Points at distance at most $4r$ from $x(I)$ satisfy $|w(s)|\leqslant Cr$. Therefore their parameters belong to the interval where $|\langle w(s),e\rangle|\leqslant Cr$, whose length is at most $4Cr/c$. This is precisely a bound on the arclength of the portion near $x(I)$. Since $|t'(s)|\leqslant C$, its projection onto $I$, and the $Cr$-neighborhood of that projection, also have length at most $Cr$.

We call these unselected passages the far arcs and choose
\begin{equation}
 r=c\delta/(1+T).
 \label{geo:radius}
\end{equation}
The part of $I$ within distance $4r$ of the far arcs has total length at most $C(1+T)r/\delta$. Choosing $c$ small makes this less than $|I|/8$.

We must also separate the positions of the selected graphs. Put $\sigma=c(1+T)^{-1}e^{-CT}$. The phase-space separation in Lemma~\ref{geo:cluster} gives $|u_i-u_0|+|u_i'-u_0'|\geqslant c\sigma$ on $I$. With $a=c\sigma/m$, Lemma~\ref{geo:graphs} shows that the union of the sets $\{|u_i-u_0|<a\}$ has length at most $Cma/\sigma<|I|/8$, after decreasing $c$. Hence the middle half of $I$ contains $t_*$ outside both exceptional sets. The ball of radius $2r$ about $x(t_*)$ misses all far arcs, and
\begin{equation}
 |u_i(t_*)-u_0(t_*)|\geqslant a,\qquad 1\leqslant i\leqslant q.
 \label{geo:goodpoint}
\end{equation}

Choose a nonnegative smooth bump $\chi_r$, equal to one on the ball of radius $r$ about $x(t_*)$ and supported in the ball of radius $2r$. In the chart, put
\begin{equation}
 F(t,y)=\chi_r(t,y)\prod_{i=1}^q|y-u_i(t)|^2,
 \label{geo:product}
\end{equation}
and extend it by zero. The empty product is one. Every passage of $\eta$ through the support lies on a selected graph. The squared factors therefore give $F|_\eta=0$ and $dF|_\eta=0$.

The graph equation bounds $\left\|u_i\right\|_{C^k}$ by a constant depending only on $k,B$: successive differentiation uses derivatives of the metric of order at most $k-1$. Since the coordinates were fixed smooth charts, the construction loses no regularity. The product rule gives
\begin{equation}
 \left\|F\right\|_{C^k}\leqslant C_{k,m,B}r^{-k}.
 \label{geo:productnorm}
\end{equation}
Furthermore, the first derivatives of all graphs have a uniform bound. Thus~\eqref{geo:goodpoint}, with $a/2$ in place of $a$, holds on an interval of length $c\min\{r,a\}$ about $t_*$. On this interval $\chi_r=1$, so
\begin{equation}
 \int_\gamma F\,ds_g\geqslant c_m\min\{r,a\}a^{2q}.
 \label{geo:positiveintegral}
\end{equation}
We normalize by setting $f=F/(C_{k,m,B}r^{-k})$, with the denominator from~\eqref{geo:productnorm}.

To compute the length derivative, recall the first-variation formula
\begin{equation}
 \left.\frac{d}{ds}\ell_{g_s}(\gamma_s)\right|_{s=0}=\frac12\int_\gamma \left.\partial_sg_s\right|_{s=0}(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)\,ds_g,
 \label{geo:firstvariation}
\end{equation}
where $\gamma$ is parametrized by $g$-arclength. The curve-variation term vanishes because $\gamma$ is a closed geodesic. Negative curvature makes the normal periodic Jacobi operator invertible, giving the local continuation in the metric; tangential changes only reparametrize the curve.

For~\eqref{geo:conformal}, the derivative is $-\tfrac12\int_\gamma f\,ds_g$. Also, $f=df=0$ on $\eta$, so the first jets of $g_s$ and $g$ agree there. The curve $\eta$ remains a geodesic of the same length. It follows from~\eqref{geo:positiveintegral} that the absolute derivative of the difference is at least
\[
 c_{k,m,B}r^k\min\{r,a\}a^{2q}.
\]
By~\eqref{geo:sparseball} and~\eqref{geo:radius},
\[
 r\geqslant c(1+T)^{-2}e^{-CT/m},\qquad a\geqslant c_m(1+T)^{-1}e^{-CT},\qquad \min\{r,a\}\geqslant c_m(1+T)^{-2}e^{-CT}.
\]
Since $q\leqslant m-1$, the resulting lower bound is
\[
 c_{k,m,B}(1+T)^{-2k-2m}\exp\left[-C\left(\frac{k}{m}+2m\right)T\right].
\]
The polynomial factor has the required exponential cost as well. Indeed, $\log(1+T)\leqslant T/m+\log(1+m)$ gives
\[
 (1+T)^{-2k}\geqslant(1+m)^{-2k}e^{-2kT/m},\qquad (1+T)^{-2m}\geqslant e^{-2mT}.
\]
Absorbing $(1+m)^{-2k}$ into the prefactor proves~\eqref{geo:detectorbound}. The same bound holds for repeated traversals. Indeed, if $\gamma$ traverses its geometric geodesic $\gamma_0$ exactly $p$ times, then
\[
 \int_\gamma f\,ds_g=p\int_{\gamma_0}f\,ds_g\geqslant\int_{\gamma_0}f\,ds_g,
\]
since $p\geqslant1$ and $f\geqslant0$. The integral along $\eta$ remains zero, regardless of its traversal number. Thus repetitions can only increase the nonzero first variation.

It remains to consider different traversal numbers of the same geometric geodesic $\gamma_0$. We take $f$ to be a fixed positive constant with $\left\|f\right\|_{C^k}\leqslant1$. If the traversal numbers are $p\ne q$, then
\[
 \ell_{g_s}(\gamma_s)-\ell_{g_s}(\eta_s)=(p-q)(1+sf)^{-1/2}\ell_g(\gamma_0),
\]
so the absolute derivative at zero is $\tfrac12 f|p-q|\ell_g(\gamma_0)\geqslant\tfrac12 f\ell_g(\gamma_0)$.

Here we use the \emph{systole} $\operatorname{sys}(g)$, the length of a shortest nontrivial closed geodesic of $g$. It is bounded below uniformly on $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}$. Indeed, after shrinking $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}$, there is $c_0>0$ such that $g\geqslant c_0h$ as quadratic forms. Every curve then has $g$-length at least $\sqrt{c_0}$ times its $h$-length. Minimizing in each free homotopy class and then over the classes gives
\begin{equation}
 \ell_g(\alpha)\geqslant\sqrt{c_0}\ell_h(\alpha),\qquad
 \operatorname{sys}(g)\geqslant\sqrt{c_0}\operatorname{sys}(h)>0.
 \label{geo:systole}
\end{equation}
The last inequality follows from the positive injectivity radius of the fixed compact manifold $(M,h)$. Thus the derivative above is at least $\tfrac12 f\sqrt{c_0}\operatorname{sys}(h)$, proving the remaining case.

label: geo:sqrt
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{geo:sqrt}
For every $k\geqslant3$, the variation in Proposition~\ref{geo:detector} can be chosen with
\[
 \left\|f\right\|_{C^k}\leqslant1,\qquad \left|\left.\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(\ell_{g_s}(\gamma_s)-\ell_{g_s}(\eta_s)\bigr)\right|_{s=0}\right|\geqslant c_{k,B}e^{-C\sqrt{k}\,T}.
\]

title: Proof
body_md: The choice $m=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$ gives $m+k/m\leqslant2\sqrt{k}+1$ in Proposition~\ref{geo:detector}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Local conformal perturbations also occur in Schenck's construction~\cite{Schenck}. Here, the product in~\eqref{geo:product} removes at most $m-1$ nearby passages exactly, while the cutoff is placed at the larger scale $e^{-CT/m}$. Their respective costs are $m$ and $k/m$ in the exponent. This is the geometric counterpart of the product and localization used in~\cite[Appendix~A, proof of Proposition~A.3]{DK}.
head: environment

label: prob:jackson
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: A fixed finite Fourier approximation

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the approximation estimate on a flat torus. Choose an even function $\Phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ equal to one near zero, with $0\leqslant\Phi\leqslant1$, and put
\[
 K(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{i x\cdot\xi}\Phi(\xi)\,d\xi.
\]
Repeated integration by parts shows that $K$ and its derivatives decay faster than every inverse power of $|x|$. Fourier inversion gives $\int K(x)\,dx=1$ and $\int x^\alpha K(x)\,dx=0$ for every multi-index with $|\alpha|\geqslant1$, because all positive-order derivatives of $\Phi$ vanish at zero. These are the standard Fourier facts used below; see~\cite[Chapter~I, Section~1]{Stein}.

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $u$, define
\[
 S_Nu(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}N^nK(Nz)u(x-z)\,dz=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Z^n}\Phi(q/N)\widehat u(q)e^{i q\cdot x}.
\]
The sum is finite. Taylor's formula to order $k-1$ and the moment identities cancel every term except the remainder. Consequently,
\[
 |S_Nu(x)-u(x)|\leqslant C_k\left\|u\right\|_{C^k}\int N^n|K(Nz)|\,|z|^k\,dz\leqslant C_kN^{-k}\left\|u\right\|_{C^k}.
\]
Also, $|\Phi(q/N)\widehat u(q)|\leqslant\left\|u\right\|_{C^0}$. The smooth frequency cutoff therefore gives the full approximation rate $N^{-k}$, without losing derivatives.

We now choose a finite smooth atlas, a subordinate partition of unity $\rho_i$, and cutoffs $\chi_i$ supported in the corresponding charts and equal to one on $\operatorname{supp}\rho_i$. After rescaling the coordinates, each $\rho_i f$, extended by zero, is a $C^k$ function on a flat torus. Let $u_i$ denote this extension and set $f_N=\sum_i\chi_i S_Nu_i$ in the charts. Since $\sum_i\chi_i u_i=f$, the preceding estimate gives the required uniform error. The fixed modes are $\chi_i\cos(q\cdot x)$ and $\chi_i\sin(q\cdot x)$, including the modes $\chi_i$ for $q=0$. With $\nu_j=1+|q|$, counting lattice points and differentiating these functions proves~\eqref{prob:modes}; the Fourier coefficient bound proves the other assertion in~\eqref{prob:jackson-estimate}. All charts, cutoffs, and modes are chosen before the metric and the geodesic pair.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Random perturbations parametrized by Hilbert bricks were used by Kaloshin--Hunt~\cite[Sections~1.3 and~2.3]{KH} to prove prevalent stretched exponential bounds for the number of periodic points of diffeomorphisms. Here, the summable Fourier weights provide a compact parameter image in finite regularity, as in the circle construction of~\cite[Appendix A.3]{DK}.
head: environment

label: prob:second-variation
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Second variation along a metric path

label: prob:coercivity
title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to calculate at $t=0$. Put $g=g_0$, $q=\partial_tg_t|_0$, and $b=\partial_t^2g_t|_0$. Parametrize the closed geodesic by $g$-arclength, write $v=\dot\gamma$, and choose the parametrizations of its continuations so that their variation $V$ is normal to $v$. The classical second-variation formula gives the index form on periodic normal fields; see~\cite[Chapter~XI, Section~1]{Lang}. In our notation, it is
\[
 I(V,W)=\int_\gamma\bigl(\langle D_sV,D_sW\rangle-\langle R(V,v)v,W\rangle\bigr)\,ds.
\]
If $-\kappa^2<0$ is a uniform upper bound for the sectional curvatures in $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}$, then
\begin{equation}
 I(V,V)\geqslant\left\|D_sV\right\|_{L^2}^2+\kappa^2\left\|V\right\|_{L^2}^2.
 \label{prob:coercivity}
\end{equation}
Thus the index form controls both the field $V$ and its covariant derivative along the geodesic. This positive lower bound is what we mean by \emph{coercivity}; its constant does not depend on the period. In particular, $\left\|V\right\|_{L^2}\leqslant\kappa^{-1}I(V,V)^{1/2}$.

Differentiating the first metric variation of length in the curve direction $W$ and integrating by parts, we obtain
\[
 B_q(W)=\frac12\int_\gamma(\nabla_Wq)(v,v)\,ds-\int_\gamma(\nabla_vq)(W,v)\,ds,\qquad |B_q(W)|\leqslant C_h\sqrt{\ell_g(\gamma)}\left\|q\right\|_{C^1}\left\|W\right\|_{L^2}.
\]
Here the arclength variation vanishes because $W$ is normal and $\gamma$ is a geodesic. Differentiation of the critical-point equation gives $I(V,W)+B_q(W)=0$. Taking $W=V$ and using~\eqref{prob:coercivity}, we get
\[
 I(V,V)\leqslant C_h\sqrt{\ell_g(\gamma)}\left\|q\right\|_{C^1}\left\|V\right\|_{L^2}\leqslant C_h\sqrt{\ell_g(\gamma)}\left\|q\right\|_{C^1}I(V,V)^{1/2}.
\]
Thus $I(V,V)\leqslant C_h\ell_g(\gamma)\left\|q\right\|_{C^1}^2$. For the critical value of length, the second derivative is
\[
 \left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\ell_{g_t}(\gamma)\right|_{t=0}=\frac12\int_\gamma b(v,v)\,ds-\frac14\int_\gamma q(v,v)^2\,ds-I(V,V).
\]
The preceding bound proves~\eqref{prob:hessian}. Estimate~\eqref{prob:coercivity} also justifies the continuation used in the calculation. Indeed, a periodic normal Jacobi field lies in the kernel of the index form, so $I(V,V)=0$, and~\eqref{prob:coercivity} forces $V=0$. The periodic normal Jacobi operator is self-adjoint and elliptic on the compact parameter circle; having zero kernel, it is invertible. The implicit function theorem therefore gives the required twice differentiable continuation for $C^k$ metrics, $k\geqslant3$, after removing the freedom of parametrization. For a multiply covered geodesic, the same argument uses its full period and the same constants.
head: environment

label: prob:small-values
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{prob:small-values}
Let $F\in C^2([-1,1]^D)$, and suppose that, at every point,
\[
 \max_{1\leqslant i\leqslant D}|\partial_iF|\geqslant b>0,\qquad |\partial_i^2F|\leqslant H\quad(1\leqslant i\leqslant D).
\]
For normalized Lebesgue measure and every $a>0$,
\[
 \mathbb P\{|F|<a\}\leqslant2D\frac{a}{b}\left(1+\frac{4H}{b}\right).
\] \qed
head: environment
name: A sublevel estimate

label: prob:pair
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: A uniform probability estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
We first retain $m$ as a parameter. Denote the lower bound in~\eqref{prob:detector} by $A_T$, and let $f$ be a separating function at the metric $g+v_\xi$. In a scalar direction $v$, the derivative of the tensor $v_\xi$ is $-(1+u_\xi)^{-2}vh$. The first variation formula~\eqref{geo:firstvariation} therefore gives the following linear functional of $v$:
\[
 -\frac12\int_\gamma\frac{v}{(1+u_\xi)^2}h(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)\,ds_{g+v_\xi}+\frac12\int_\eta\frac{v}{(1+u_\xi)^2}h(\dot\eta,\dot\eta)\,ds_{g+v_\xi}.
\]
Its norm on $C^0(M)$ is at most $C_hT$. To recover the direction $fh$, we take $\widehat f=-(1+u_\xi)^2f$, whose $C^k$ norm is uniformly bounded by $C_k$ on the parameter cube.

We approximate $\widehat f$ by the fixed modes from Lemma~\ref{prob:jackson}. Choose the least integer $N\geqslant2$ such that
\begin{equation}
 N^k\geqslant C_kT/A_T.
 \label{prob:cutoff}
\end{equation}
Then $\widehat f_N=\sum_{\nu_j\leqslant CN}b_je_j$ has $|b_j|\leqslant C_k$, and its value under the displayed functional has modulus at least $A_T/2$. Indeed, the approximation changes that value by at most $C_hT\left\|\widehat f-\widehat f_N\right\|_{C^0}\leqslant A_T/2$, after increasing the constant in~\eqref{prob:cutoff}. There are at most $CN^n$ terms, so at least one direction $-(1+u_\xi)^{-2}e_jh$ gives a length derivative of modulus at least $A_T/(C_kN^n)$. Including its weight in~\eqref{prob:probe}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
 |\partial_{\xi_j}(\ell_\gamma-\ell_\eta)|\geqslant b_T:=c_k\varepsilon A_TN^{-(k+2n+2)},\qquad \nu_j\leqslant CN.
 \label{prob:coordinate}
\end{equation}
This choice is made separately at each parameter. We do not differentiate the separating function or its Fourier coefficients. Although the selected index can vary, its finite list and the lower bound $b_T$ are fixed throughout the parameter cube.

Let us now bound the second derivatives with respect to these coordinates. Direct differentiation gives
\[
 \partial_{\xi_j}v_\xi=-\varepsilon\nu_j^{-(k+n+2)}\frac{e_jh}{(1+u_\xi)^2},\qquad \partial_{\xi_j}^2v_\xi=2\varepsilon^2\nu_j^{-2(k+n+2)}\frac{e_j^2h}{(1+u_\xi)^3}.
\]
By~\eqref{prob:modes}, $\left\|u_\xi\right\|_{C^1}\leqslant C_h\varepsilon$ uniformly in $k\geqslant3$. Since $1+u_\xi\geqslant1/2$, the product rule gives $\left\|\partial_{\xi_j}v_\xi\right\|_{C^1}\leqslant C_h\varepsilon$ and $\left\|\partial_{\xi_j}^2v_\xi\right\|_{C^0}\leqslant C_h\varepsilon^2$. Consequently, for $F(\xi)=\ell_{g+v_\xi}(\gamma)-\ell_{g+v_\xi}(\eta)$, Lemma~\ref{prob:second-variation} implies
\[
 |\partial_{\xi_j}^2F|\leqslant C_hT\varepsilon^2.
\]
The acceleration term in~\eqref{prob:hessian} accounts for the nonlinear parametrization of the probe.

We condition on all coordinates with $\nu_j>CN$. For every fixed tail, $F$ is a $C^2$ function of at most $CN^n$ remaining coordinates. Its maximal first derivative is at least $b_T$ by~\eqref{prob:coordinate}, and the preceding second-derivative bound is uniform in the tail. Lemma~\ref{prob:small-values}, followed by integration over the tail, yields
\[
 \mathbb P\{|F|<a\}\leqslant CN^n\frac{a}{b_T}\left(1+\frac{C_hT\varepsilon^2}{b_T}\right).
\]
In particular, no measurable choice of the separating coordinate is needed.

It remains to keep track of the exponential cost. Put $X=m+k/m$, so that $A_T=a_{k,m}e^{-C_hXT}$. The choice~\eqref{prob:cutoff} and the definition of $b_T$ give
\[
 N^n\leqslant C_{k,m}T^{n/k}e^{C_hXnT/k},\qquad b_T^{-1}\leqslant C_{k,m,\varepsilon}T^{1+(2n+2)/k}e^{C_hX(2+(2n+2)/k)T}.
\]
Combining these bounds with the preceding probability estimate, and enlarging the prefactor to include the term containing only $b_T^{-1}$, we obtain
\[
 \mathbb P\{|F|<a\}\leqslant C_{k,m,\varepsilon}a\,T^{3+(5n+4)/k}e^{C_hX(4+(5n+4)/k)T}.
\]
For $k\geqslant3$, the coefficients involving $1/k$ are bounded in terms of the dimension alone. The polynomial in $T$ can also be absorbed into a fixed additional exponential because $T\geqslant1$ and $X\geqslant2$. Thus the last expression is at most $C_{k,m,\varepsilon}a e^{C_hXT}$, after increasing $C_h$ independently of $k$ and $m$. Finally, taking $m=\lceil\sqrt{k}\rceil$, as in Corollary~\ref{geo:sqrt}, gives $X\leqslant2\sqrt{k}+1$ and proves~\eqref{prob:pair-bound}.

name: Almost sure exponential gaps

title: Proof
body_md:
In this proof, $C,H,B$ depend on the fixed metric $h$ and its chosen geometric neighborhood, but not on $k$. We first count the classes that can occur below a given length. There are at most $Ce^{HT}$ classes of $h$-length at most $T$. Indeed, choosing a compact fundamental domain in the universal cover, a closed geodesic of length at most $T$ gives a deck transformation, after conjugation, moving a fixed basepoint by at most $T+C$. Cocompactness allows us to divide a joining geodesic into bounded segments and choose nearby orbit points. Successive orbit points differ by an element of a fixed finite set, so the deck transformation is a word of length at most $C(T+1)$ in a fixed finite alphabet. Counting words proves the asserted upper bound, including iterates.

Fix an integer $N\geqslant1$. Uniform equivalence with $h$ implies that a class with length at most $N$ at one parameter has $h$-length at most $CN$, and hence length at most $C^2N$ at every parameter. There are at most $Ce^{HN}$ such candidate classes, after changing $H$. Proposition~\ref{prob:pair}, with $T=C^2N$, and the union bound therefore give
\[
 \mathbb P\left\{\begin{array}{c}\text{some two classes of lengths at most }N\\\text{have a gap smaller than }e^{-\beta N}\end{array}\right\}\leqslant C_{k,\varepsilon}\exp\bigl[(C\sqrt{k}+2H-\beta)N\bigr]
\]
for all sufficiently large $N$. Pairs of different powers of the same geometric geodesic do not contribute once $e^{-\beta N}$ is below the uniform systole bound~\eqref{geo:systole}.

We choose $B>C+2H+1$ and set $\beta=B\sqrt{k}$. The probabilities are summable. By the first Borel--Cantelli lemma, almost surely every pair of length at most $N$ has gap at least $e^{-\beta N}$ for all sufficiently large integers $N$.

We also need to exclude exact equalities among the finitely many shorter geodesics. For any fixed pair of different geometric geodesics, the two lengths are bounded on the compact probe cube. Letting $a\downarrow0$ in~\eqref{prob:pair-bound} shows that their equality has probability zero. There are countably many pairs, so almost surely none of these equalities occurs. The remaining pairs below the random cutoff from Borel--Cantelli are finite in number and have positive gaps. Reducing $c(g)>0$ includes them. For a pair with maximum length $L$, the choice $N=\lceil L\rceil$ gives $e^{-\beta N}\geqslant e^{-\beta}e^{-\beta L}$, which proves~\eqref{prob:gap-property}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first identify the correspondence with the circle argument in~\cite[Appendix A]{DK}. The transverse separation estimate~\eqref{geo:hitsep} plays the role of~\cite[Lemma~3.3]{DK}, while the extreme-neighbour conclusion in Lemma~\ref{geo:cluster} corresponds to Lemma~A.1. The first variation formula~\eqref{geo:firstvariation} and Lemma~\ref{prob:second-variation} play the role of Lemma~A.2. Proposition~\ref{geo:detector}, followed by the Fourier approximation in Lemma~\ref{prob:jackson} and the extraction of a coordinate in~\eqref{prob:coordinate}, corresponds to Proposition~A.3. Lemma~\ref{prob:small-values} is its Lemma~A.4. Proposition~\ref{prob:gaps} supplies the probability-one conclusion obtained there in Appendix~A.4. We now complete the proof by the translation argument of Appendix~A.5, keeping track of arbitrary tensor translations.

First, the asserted set is Borel. Indeed, the set of unoriented free homotopy classes is countable, and the length in each class is continuous in the metric. For $\beta=B\sqrt{k}$, the set is
\[
 \bigcup_{q=1}^\infty\ \bigcap_{\gamma\ne\eta}\left\{g\in\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}\cap C^k:|\ell_g(\gamma)-\ell_g(\eta)|\geqslant q^{-1}e^{-\beta\max\{\ell_g(\gamma),\ell_g(\eta)\}}\right\}.
\]
Each condition in the intersection is closed relative to $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}\cap C^k$. Denote the complement of this Borel set in $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}\cap C^k$ by $E$.

We next prove that $E$ is shy locally. Choose a $C^k$-ball $B(g_0,r)$ with $B(g_0,3r)\subset\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}$, and take the probe~\eqref{prob:probe} with compact support $K$ contained in the radius-$r$ ball about zero. For any tensor $a$, suppose that $(a+K)\cap B(g_0,r)$ is nonempty, and choose $v_0\in K$ with $a+v_0\in B(g_0,r)$. Every $v\in K$ then satisfies
\[
 \left\|a+v-g_0\right\|_{C^k}\leqslant\left\|a+v_0-g_0\right\|_{C^k}+\left\|v-v_0\right\|_{C^k}<3r.
\]
The whole translated family lies in the bounded ball $B(g_0,3r)$. Proposition~\ref{prob:gaps} therefore gives $\mathbb P\{a+v_\xi\in E\cap B(g_0,r)\}=0$. If the translated support does not meet the smaller ball, the same equality is immediate. Thus the law of $v_\xi$ witnesses shyness of $E\cap B(g_0,r)$ for every tensor translation $a$. The translated metrics need not remain in one conformal class.

Since $C^k(S^2T^*M)$ is separable, countably many such smaller balls cover $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}\cap C^k$. Let $E_j$ be the corresponding exceptional pieces. We finish by constructing one witness for their union. For each $j$, choose a random tensor $w_j$ witnessing shyness of $E_j$, with compact support of radius at most $2^{-j}$. This is possible because the probe size $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary. Choose these tensors independently. The series $w=\sum_jw_j$ converges uniformly over the product of their supports, since its tail norm is at most $\sum_{j>L}2^{-j}$. Its sum is consequently a continuous image of a compact product, and its law has compact support.

For a fixed translation $a$ and an index $j$, conditioning on all $w_i$ with $i\ne j$ leaves one fixed translation of $w_j$. Its witnessing property gives
\[
 \mathbb P\left\{a+\sum_iw_i\in E_j\,\middle|\,(w_i)_{i\ne j}\right\}=0.
\]
Integration over the conditioned variables, followed by the countable union over $j$, shows that $\mathbb P\{a+w\in E\}=0$ for every $a$. This proves prevalence in $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}\cap C^k$.

Finally, every nonempty $C^k$-ball contained in $\operatorname{{\mathscr U}}$ contains a translate of an arbitrarily small probe. Proposition~\ref{prob:gaps} provides a metric satisfying~\eqref{prob:gap-property} in that ball. The asserted set is therefore dense.
